blocks.html: Categorical data, such as blood group, nutritional status or CBHI membership, have no continuous scale, so each category gets its own separate bar or wedge. The same diagrams also suit ungrouped discrete counts, such as the number of ANC visits (recall §1.4.2); continuous data need a histogram instead (§4.3.1). By convention the bars stand apart with gaps, which tells the reader that the categories are separate classes, whether they are unordered (water source) or ordered (normal, moderate, severe wasting). The two standard forms are the bar diagram (§4.2.1) and the pie diagram (§4.2.2).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A bar diagram represents each category by a rectangular bar whose length (or height) is proportional to the frequency, or to some other value, of that category.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
To compare “how many” across categories, draw one bar per category, make its length proportional to the count, and let the eye compare lengths. Three variants are used:

  • Simple bar: one bar per category of one variable.
  • Multiple (grouped) bar: bars for subgroups stand side by side within each category, for example boys and girls within each age group.
  • Component (stacked) bar: each bar is divided into segments for the subgroups, so it shows the total and its make-up at once. When every bar is scaled to 100%, it becomes a percentage (100%) component bar, which compares the make-up of groups of different sizes.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why must the value axis start at zero? A bar of value a drawn from a baseline c has length a − c. For two bars, a and b:

drawn ratio = (b − c) ÷ (a − c)

This equals the true ratio b ÷ a only when c = 0. If 0 < c < a < b, the drawn ratio is always larger than the true one, so a raised baseline always exaggerates the difference. The CDC’s teaching text states that breaks in the scale should not be used in bar charts (CDC, 2012a). §4.5.6 works through a numeric example.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the under-five clinic register of 100 children, 60 have normal nutritional status, 25 moderate wasting and 15 severe wasting. Three bars show at once that severe wasting is the smallest group.

blocks.alt: Bar diagram of nutritional status at an under-five clinic
blocks.caption: Figure 4.1. Simple bar diagram: nutritional status of the 100 children in the under-five clinic register.

blocks.html: Now split the same 100 children by wealth quintile (Q1 poorest).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Quintile sizes are unequal: Q1 13, Q2 26, Q3 21, Q4 20, Q5 20 children. In a component bar of counts (Figure 4.2, left) the Q2 bar is twice as tall as the Q1 bar, so the eye compares totals, not make-up.
  2. Convert each segment to a percentage of its own bar. In Q1, 1 of 13 children is normal: 1 ÷ 13 × 100 = 7.7%. Severe wasting in Q1: 6 ÷ 13 × 100 = 46.2%.
  3. In Q2, 9 of 26 are normal: 34.6%. In Q3, 15 of 21: 71.4%. In Q4, 15 of 20: 75.0%. In Q5, 20 of 20: 100%.
  4. Result: in the percentage bar (Figure 4.2, right) every bar has the same height, so the gradient in normal status, from 7.7% in the poorest quintile to 100% in the richest, is plain to see.

blocks.alt: Component and percentage bar diagrams of nutritional status by wealth quintile
blocks.caption: Figure 4.2. Component bar (counts, left) and percentage component bar (right): nutritional status by wealth quintile, under-five clinic register (n = 100).

points.html: Use a component bar of counts when the totals matter, and a percentage bar when you want to compare composition across groups of different sizes. The CDC describes the 100% component bar as useful “for comparing the contribution of different subgroups within the categories” (CDC, 2012a).
Only the bottom segment of a stacked bar sits on a common baseline. The other segments float, so they are harder to compare across bars; put the segment you most want compared at the bottom.
With many categories a bar diagram becomes cluttered. Order the bars by size (unless the categories have a natural order), draw them horizontally, or use a table.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A pie diagram is a circle divided into wedges whose angles (and therefore areas) are proportional to each category’s share of the total. It shows how one whole divides into parts.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A bar diagram compares magnitudes; a pie diagram answers “what share of the whole?”. Each wedge’s central angle is:

angle = (category frequency ÷ total) × 360°

So the full circle is always 100%.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The pie in Figure 4.3 shows the water source of surveyed households: piped water 45%, well 30%, river 15% and other 10%. The “other” wedge is what makes the categories exhaustive; without it the wedges would not add to the whole circle.

blocks.alt: Pie diagram of household water source
blocks.caption: Figure 4.3. Pie diagram of household water source (% of surveyed households), drawn from 12 o’clock, largest to smallest clockwise.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
In the CBHI survey, 350 households did not join the scheme. Their reasons were lack of knowledge 112, lack of money 98, lack of trust 67, bad image 46, other 27.

  1. Lack of knowledge: 112 ÷ 350 × 360° = 115.2°.
  2. Lack of money: 98 ÷ 350 × 360° = 100.8°.
  3. Lack of trust: 67 ÷ 350 × 360° = 68.9°.
  4. Bad image: 46 ÷ 350 × 360° = 47.3°.
  5. Other: 27 ÷ 350 × 360° = 27.8°.
  6. Check: 115.2 + 100.8 + 68.9 + 47.3 + 27.8 = 360.0°. The shares are 32.0%, 28.0%, 19.1%, 13.1% and 7.7%.

points.html: A pie needs categories that are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, adding to 100%. A bar diagram does not have this requirement.

People judge angles and areas less accurately than lengths or positions on a common scale. Cleveland and McGill ranked “position along a common scale” first and angle and area lower, and concluded that “a pie chart can always be replaced by a bar chart” (Cleveland & McGill, 1984). Pie diagrams remain common in reports, so you must be able to read and draw them.

Choose between the two by the question, not only by the number of categories. If the reader must compare categories with each other (is lack of money as common as lack of knowledge?), use bars. If the single message is the share of one whole, a pie with a few wedges can work.
A common construction convention: start at 12 o’clock, order wedges from largest to smallest clockwise, and label each wedge with its percentage (CDC, 2012a).

questions.prompt: The five reasons for not joining CBHI (112, 98, 67, 46 and 27 households) are to go in your thesis. You want the reader to compare the reasons with one another. Would a bar diagram or a pie diagram serve better, and why?
questions.answer: A bar diagram. The purpose is to compare categories with each other, and the eye compares lengths on a common baseline more accurately than angles or areas (Cleveland & McGill, 1984). The number of categories is not the deciding point: five exhaustive categories (they include “other” and add to 350) could be drawn as a pie, and a pie would suit a message about the share of one whole. For “which reason is most common, and by how much?”, bars ordered from largest to smallest are clearer.

questions.prompt: Why must a bar diagram’s value axis start at zero? Use the drawn-ratio formula to show what happens if it starts at 50 for two bars of 60 and 80.
questions.answer: A bar encodes its value by its length, so lengths are in the right ratio only if they are measured from zero. From baseline c = 50: drawn ratio = (80 − 50) ÷ (60 − 50) = 30 ÷ 10 = 3. True ratio = 80 ÷ 60 = 1.33. The truncated chart makes the second bar look three times the first, when it is only one-third larger.

questions.prompt: In Figure 4.2, Q3 has 15 normal, 4 moderately wasted and 2 severely wasted children. What height does the moderate-wasting segment have in the percentage bar?
questions.answer: Q3 total = 15 + 4 + 2 = 21. Moderate wasting = 4 ÷ 21 × 100 = 19.0%. The segment runs from 71.4% (the top of the normal segment, 15/21) to 71.4 + 19.0 = 90.5%.
